target_claim: Running the (revisiting-allowed) Dijkstra variant on the explicitly constructed Gn yields Omega(2^n) Relax operations; in particular the relaxations of edges vi->vn alone produce 2^{n-2}-1 distinct updates to d(vn).
source_quote:
There
are 2 n−2 −1 nonempty subsets of {v2, . . . , vn−1}, so the edge relaxations vi →vn (for
i = 2, 3, . . . , n −1) account for 2 n−2 −1 updates to vn’s distance alone. Even excluding
the source’s initial relaxations and all the intermediate-to-intermediate relaxations, we
already have Ω(2n) relaxations.
test_sketch: Implement Gn exactly as specified (vertices v1..vn; edges v1->vn weight W, v1->vi weight 0, vi->vn weight W-delta_i, vi->vj weight -delta_i for 2<=i<j<=n-1, delta_i = 2^{i-2}, W = sum delta_i) and the described modified Dijkstra (min-heap, vertices may be re-inserted/revisited when their tentative distance improves), ~60 lines of Python. Instrument two counters: total Relax operations and number of successful updates to d(vn). Run for n = 5..12. The solution's own trace shows each vertex settles once in order v2,...,v{n-1}, so d(vn) is updated exactly n-2 times (e.g. 8 for n=10, vs the claimed 2^8-1 = 255) and total relaxations are Theta(n^2) (~(n-1)(n-2)/2 + n, e.g. ~45 for n=10, vs claimed >= 2^{n-2} = 256), growing quadratically not exponentially across n. Operation counts, no wall clock. The solution even concedes 'the overall relaxation count is Theta(n^2)' at line 0206, contradicting its own claimed lower bound; the instrumented run certifies which statement holds.
